y-m-76-12.title: Sales were high on days we handed out many flyers: was it because of flyers?
y-m-76-12.topic: Data interpretation: moving together and cause
y-m-76-12.goal: Check whether two quantities moving together means cause and effect; describe a comparison that rules out other explanations.
y-m-76-12.material:
Small-shop owner records flyers handed out this week and same-day sales.
Mon: 0 flyers, sales 50만 원
Tue: 0, sales 52만 원
Wed: 100, sales 51만 원
Thu: 100, sales 49만 원
Fri: 200, sales 80만 원
Sat: 300, sales 120만 원
Sun: 300, sales 118만 원
Owner says, 'More flyers on a day, higher sales. Flyers raise sales, so let's double flyers next month.' Shop is in area where weekend customers increase, and owner handed out more flyers to match weekends.
y-m-76-12.thinking.1: Choosing comparison that makes cause more convincing
y-m-76-12.thinking.2: Saying what to check before deciding
y-m-76-12.prereq.1: Reading table and whether two quantities rise/fall together
y-m-76-12.s.s1.prompt: What is best judgment about concluding from table alone that flyers raised sales?
y-m-76-12.s.s1.hint.0: List all weekdays with many flyers.
y-m-76-12.s.s1.hint.1: Among same kind of days (Mon–Thu), compare sales for days with different flyer counts.
y-m-76-12.s.s1.o.a: Sales high on all seven days with many flyers, so flyers caused it.
y-m-76-12.s.s1.r.a: Same pattern doesn't prove cause. Another reason, like weekend customers, may move both quantities.
y-m-76-12.s.s1.o.b: Not enough to conclude. Many flyers overlap with busy weekend.
y-m-76-12.s.s1.o.c: On Mon–Thu flyers and sales aren't related, so we can conclude flyers have no effect.
y-m-76-12.s.s1.r.c: Mon–Thu flyer counts only 0 or 100, so comparison is limited; can't conclude no effect.
y-m-76-12.s.s1.o.d: Only 7 days data, so table tells nothing.
y-m-76-12.s.s1.r.d: Even with little data, table reveals another explanation: weekend customers.
y-m-76-12.s.s1.explain: Days with many flyers (Fri, Sat, Sun) overlap weekend when customer count rises. Mon–Thu sales almost same with 0 and 100 flyers. Table alone can't separate flyer effect from weekend effect.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.prompt: Choose all ways to check more reliably if flyers raise sales.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.hint.0: Think why flyer and no-flyer days should be same day of week when compared.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.hint.1: Mark each option that filters out non-flyer explanations.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.o.a: Separate weekends and weekdays; compare flyer/no-flyer days of same kind.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.o.b: Pick only highest-sales day and check flyers.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.r.b: Looking at one top day can't separate it from other conditions that day. Need comparison.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.o.c: Alternate flyer days regardless of weekday and compare sales over several weeks.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.o.d: Only calculate average sales for flyer days.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.r.d: Without comparing no-flyer days, can't identify flyer effect.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.explain: Compare same type of day or alternate flyer days so weekday effect doesn't mix in; this helps isolate flyer impact.
y-m-76-12.s.s3.prompt: Suggest one check owner should do before deciding to double flyers next month, and why.
y-m-76-12.s.s3.hint.0: Check again which weekdays have many versus few flyers.
y-m-76-12.s.s3.hint.1: Say which weekday data needed to compare same weekdays only.
y-m-76-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does my proposed check separate weekend effect from flyer effect?
y-m-76-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you consider time or cost of the check?
y-m-76-12.s.s3.model.0: Days with many flyers are weekends, when customers may already be plentiful. Before deciding, compare same weekday with and without flyers.
y-m-76-12.s.s3.model.1: First vary flyer counts on weekdays over several weeks. Current table overlaps flyers with weekend, so we can't tell flyer effect from weekend customers.

y-m-76-08.prereq.0: Assumption: try after middle-school maths. H2 only difficulty label meaning analysis one step more careful than H1, not grade assignment.
y-m-76-08.title: If 1 of 50 inspected parts is defective, are there 100 defectives in whole box?
y-m-76-08.topic: Sample survey: using sample defect rate to talk about whole
y-m-76-08.goal: Sample ratio is one estimate of population ratio. Work out which population ratios fit this result and what else must be known.
y-m-76-08.material:
A parts factory box has 5,000 parts. Inspector randomly checks 50 and finds 1 defective (sample rate 2%). Manager reports, 'This box has 100 defectives.' Table below shows chance that, if true whole-box defect rate were this, at most 1 defective appears among 50 random checks (calculated beforehand).
Rate 1%: about 91.1%; 2%: 73.6%; 5%: 27.9%; 8%: 8.3%; 12%: 1.3%.
y-m-76-08.thinking.0: Sorting what sample result can and can't tell
y-m-76-08.thinking.1: Using table to judge possible range for whole ratio
y-m-76-08.prereq.1: Ratios and percentages; multiplying total by ratio
y-m-76-08.prereq.2: Probability is number from 0 to 1 expressing 'chance of happening' (middle-school level)
y-m-76-08.s.s1.prompt: What is best evaluation of manager's report '100 defectives'?
y-m-76-08.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate how many percentage points separate getting 1 defective and getting 2 in sample of 50.
y-m-76-08.s.s1.hint.1: Give one reason whole defect rate can differ even if sample rate same.
y-m-76-08.s.s1.o.a: Sample only 1% of box, so result gives no clue about whole.
y-m-76-08.s.s1.r.a: More important than sample's percent of whole are sample size and how it was drawn. It doesn't mean no clue at all.
y-m-76-08.s.s1.o.b: Sample rate 2% is whole defect rate, so exactly 100 parts defective.
y-m-76-08.s.s1.r.b: You treated sample result as exactly same as whole. A different random 50 could give another result.
y-m-76-08.s.s1.o.c: Whole rate could be above or below 2%; 100 is just one estimate.
y-m-76-08.s.s1.o.d: Whole rate might be higher than 2%, but almost no chance it is lower.
y-m-76-08.s.s1.r.d: Nothing in sample supports 'almost no chance' it is lower. Getting 1 could happen by chance too.
y-m-76-08.s.s1.explain: The 100 found by multiplying sample rate 2% is one estimate. At other whole defect rates too, getting at most 1 out of 50 can happen readily.
y-m-76-08.s.s2.prompt: Say any whole defect rate with table chance at least 10% 'does not conflict with this sample'. Select all rates not conflicting.
y-m-76-08.s.s2.hint.0: Mark table rows where chance exceeds 10%.
y-m-76-08.s.s2.hint.1: For each marked rate, convert it to defect count out of 5,000.
y-m-76-08.s.s2.r.d: At 8%, chance of at most 1 is about 8.3%, below 10%. You compared value with cutoff incorrectly.
y-m-76-08.s.s2.r.e: At 12%, chance at most 1 is about 1.3%, very low. You didn't read table values.
y-m-76-08.s.s2.explain: Among table values, 1%, 2%, 5% have likelihoods 91.1%, 73.6%, 27.9%, all at least 10%. 8% and 12% below 10%. So up to around 250 defects (5%) doesn't conflict. Table alone can't judge rates not shown.
y-m-76-08.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite report to manager. Include uncertainty in sentence and what else to do for a more precise answer.
y-m-76-08.s.s3.hint.0: Write smallest and largest non-conflicting rates from table.
y-m-76-08.s.s3.hint.1: Give one way to change inspection to narrow range.
y-m-76-08.s.s3.placeholder: Example: This box has ... defective parts ...
y-m-76-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you avoid stating '100' as fact and use range or say estimate?
y-m-76-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you guess why increasing sample size helps?
y-m-76-08.s.s3.model.0: Estimated defects about 100, but only 50 checked, so even around 250 doesn't conflict. Check about 200 randomly selected parts or repeat random sampling and compare; range will narrow.
y-m-76-08.s.s3.model.1: We can't claim exactly 100 defects. One found could be chance; inspect more at random, see whether similar rate appears, and report a range. 100 1
y-m-76-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: Variation suggesting method without absolute claim
y-m-76-08.s.s3.model.2: Since 1 defect appeared in sample of 50, 100 is only estimate, and rates 1% to 5% don't conflict. Increase number inspected.

y-m-76-07.title: Is promo 'average delivery 4 days' trustworthy?
y-m-76-07.topic: Mean and median: reading delivery-day data
y-m-76-07.goal: Check how one extreme value affects mean; choose representative measure and notice wording suited to situation.
y-m-76-07.material: Online shop wants promote 'average delivery 4 days'. Ten latest delivery times (unordered) are 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 18 days. Count whole days from order date to arrival. 4 10 1 2 3 18
y-m-76-07.thinking.0: Choosing representative value suited to info again
y-m-76-07.thinking.1: Making data where mean and median differ
y-m-76-07.prereq.0: Assumption: try after middle-school maths. H2 only difficulty label meaning analysis one step more careful than H1, not grade assignment.
y-m-76-07.prereq.1: Mean, median and mode meanings/calculation (middle-school level)
y-m-76-07.s.s1.prompt: Revise judgment 'how many days usually if order from this shop?' every time more information arrives.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.hint.0: Write data on one line in size order and find middle value.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate mean for 9 orders excluding 18 days; compare with first mean.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.0.info: Only promo 'average delivery 4 days' known. Spread of 10 data points unknown.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.0.after: Both expecting around 4 days from mean alone and holding judgment open because spread unknown have reasons now. 4
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Mean 4 days, so generally expect about 4 days.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Without knowing spread, hard to say usual delivery time.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I expect much longer than 4 days.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Mean alone doesn't support thinking it takes much longer.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: Looking at data, what is most fitting 'usual number of days'?
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.1.after: Ordered by size, middle two values 2 and 3, so median 2.5 days; 9 of 10 arrive within 4 days. One 18-day delivery pulled mean up to 4.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You call the single largest value usual, but it is only 1 of 10.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: One 18 pulls up mean. 9 of 10 within 4 days.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.2.info: Shop owner says: '18-day delivery was when typhoon blocked transport; that happened only once in past year.'
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.2.after: If exceptions rare, use number representing most people's experience. Honestly mention exceptional delays too.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Mean 4 pulled up by single 18. If unusual, customers expect longer than actual experience.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Use most people's experience, such as '9 of 10 orders arrive within 4 days'.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Also state exception, like 'mostly within 4 days; typhoon may cause delay'.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.reflect: At first we judged from mean only. Full data showed mean doesn't represent usual; last info (rare event) changed best wording. Separate info that changed 'value' from info that changed 'wording choice'.
y-m-76-07.s.s2.prompt: Set delivery days for 5 orders smallest first as a≤b≤c≤d≤e. Make 2 different sets with mean 4 days and median (middle c) 2 days or less. (All integers 1 to 30 days)
y-m-76-07.s.s2.hint.0: First determine what sum of five values needed for mean 4 days.
y-m-76-07.s.s2.hint.1: Think which position to put remaining sum in while keeping middle value small.
y-m-76-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Every value must be integer from 1 to 30.
y-m-76-07.s.s2.explain: If mean 4, sum 20. To keep middle value low, put remaining amount in one large value. Example: 1, 1, 2, 2, 14 sums to 20 and median 2.
y-m-76-07.s.s3.prompt: Write one-line delivery notice for shop. Also say what number you use instead of (or with) mean and why.
y-m-76-07.s.s3.hint.0: Arrange data by size and count orders arriving within 4 days.
y-m-76-07.s.s3.hint.1: In one sentence, say why using this number gives customers a more accurate expectation than mean.
y-m-76-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Can I find my number in the 10 order data above?
y-m-76-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say what expectation wording 'mean is 4 days' gives customers?
y-m-76-07.s.s3.model.0: 9 of 10 orders arrive within 4 days (median 2.5 days). One 18-day order pulled mean up to 4, so it is longer than most people's experience.
y-m-76-07.s.s3.model.1: Most arrive in 2 to 3 days, though rare delays happen. One very late delivery pulls mean up and doesn't represent usual delivery well.

y-m-76-03.prereq.0: Assumption: introductory task to try after finishing middle-school maths. H1 na only difficulty label for this batch, no be assignment for any class.
y-m-76-03.title: A bottle label says 'dilute 1:10': how many mL concentrate is that?
y-m-76-03.topic: Ratios and rates: reading dilution notation
y-m-76-03.goal: Know that same ratio notation can mean different amounts depending what it compares; decide amounts and clarify notation with needed information and measuring conditions.
y-m-76-03.material: There is germicide concentrate in cleaning-supply store. Bottle label only says 'dilute 1:10 before use'. We want make 1 L (1,000 mL) diluted solution. Solution is concentrate mixed with water only; assume total volume equals sum of both volumes.
y-m-76-03.thinking.1: Updating judgment as new info arrive
y-m-76-03.prereq.1: Meaning of ratio and rate, proportional expressions (first-year middle-school level)
y-m-76-03.prereq.2: Relationship between L and mL (1 L = 1,000 mL)
y-m-76-03.s.s1.prompt: Can label wording alone decide how many mL concentrate to use?
y-m-76-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write at least two ways to read 1:10.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.hint.1: For each interpretation, estimate concentrate amount for 1 L and compare.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.o.a: Can't decide. Need know what 1 and 10 in 1:10 each stand for.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.o.b: Can decide. For 1:10, concentrate is one-tenth of total, so 100 mL.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.r.b: You read 1:10 as 'concentrate : total'. You didn't leave open 'concentrate : water'.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.o.c: Can decide. There are 10 parts water to 1 part concentrate, so about 91 mL.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.r.c: 'Concentrate : water' reading possible, but unless label says so you chose one reading only.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.o.d: Can't decide. Need container size to know concentrate amount.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.r.d: You name needed info, but it doesn't concern ratio meaning. We already know make 1 L.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.explain: If 1:10 means 'concentrate : water', concentrate is 1000 ÷ 11 ≈ 91 mL; if 'concentrate : total', it's 100 mL. They differ. Without label clarifying, can't choose one.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.prompt: Update judgment about concentrate amount each time new information comes.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.hint.0: For each step, write in one line what new information settled.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.hint.1: For each option, calculate concentrate share (concentrate ÷ 1,000) and compare with standard 9.09%.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.0.info: Label only says 'dilute 1:10'. Estimate concentrate needed for 1 L.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.0.ask: What is a fitting judgment now?
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.0.after: a and b calculations pick one interpretation; c leaves both open. At this point, all can be supported with reasons.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.0.o.c: Could be 91 mL or 100 mL, so can't decide yet.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.1.info: We found small print on back: 'Add 10 parts water to 1 part concentrate and mix.'
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.1.after: With 1 part concentrate and 10 parts water, total 11 parts, so concentrate 1000 ÷ 11 ≈ 90.9 mL.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.1.r.a: This is value from reading 1:10 as concentrate : total. Back label says 10 parts water are 'added'.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.1.r.b: This value assumes concentrate : water = 1 : 9. It says water is 10 parts.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.2.info: On site there's only measuring cup marked every 10 mL. If concentrate is below 1/11 total (about 9.09%), disinfection is insufficient.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.2.ask: How much concentrate should we add?
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.2.after: 100 mL is 10%, above standard and matches cup mark. Around 91 mL is accurate but hard to measure exactly. Since it must not be below standard, rounding up is safe.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.2.r.a: 90 mL is 9% of total, below standard (about 9.09%).
y-m-76-03.s.s2.reflect: First two amounts came from different readings; wording on back settled interpretation; finally measuring tool and condition 'must not fall short' changed final amount. Separate whether information changed the 'amount' or the 'condition'.
y-m-76-03.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite label so no misunderstanding. Make one line workers can read and follow straight away.
y-m-76-03.s.s3.hint.0: Add words saying what '1' and '10' each refer to.
y-m-76-03.s.s3.hint.1: Would adding a numerical example in parentheses make it clearer?
y-m-76-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: If someone reads only this wording, can they calculate concentrate amount for 1 L?
y-m-76-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you reread it to check no other interpretation remains?
y-m-76-03.s.s3.model.0: Mix 10 parts water with 1 part concentrate. (Example: 100 mL concentrate + 1,000 mL water = 1,100 mL solution)
y-m-76-03.s.s3.model.1: Concentrate : water = 1 : 10. For each cup concentrate, use 10 cups water. To make 1 L, use about 91 mL concentrate and 909 mL water. 1 10 91 909
y-m-76-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: A variation that writes amounts too

y-m-76-10.prereq.0: Assumption: try after middle-school maths. H2 only difficulty label meaning analysis one step more careful than H1, not grade assignment.
y-m-76-10.title: When making new product codes, how many letters and digits should we use?
y-m-76-10.topic: Counting possibilities: designing a code system
y-m-76-10.goal: Understand how number of codes depends on sequential choices at each position, and make several designs satisfying count and length requirements.
y-m-76-10.material: We're making warehouse product codes. Code has a uppercase letters first, then d digits (e.g. a=2,d=3 gives KT482). Use 24 letters excluding O and I; each digit has 0–9 options. Three rules: total possible codes at least 30,000 items needed, no more than 600,000 to avoid too many unused codes, and length a+d at most 5.
y-m-76-10.thinking.0: Finding wrong line in a calculation
y-m-76-10.prereq.1: Basic counting principle (middle-school level): number of ordered choices
y-m-76-10.s.s1.prompt: Staff calculated codes for a=2,d=2 below. Choose first incorrect line.
y-m-76-10.s.s1.hint.0: Suppose first letter fixed; count options for second letter.
y-m-76-10.s.s1.hint.1: Write a few codes for small case (1 letter, 1 digit) and compare staff method.
y-m-76-10.s.s1.line.0: 24 choices for first letter, and also 24 choices for second.
y-m-76-10.s.s1.line.1: 10 choices for first digit, and also 10 for second.
y-m-76-10.s.s1.explain: Line 3 wrong. Even after choosing one position, next still has all choices available, so multiply sequentially, don't add counts. 24×24×10×10=57,600. Line 4 conclusion came from wrong count, so correct count changes it.
y-m-76-10.s.s2.prompt: Give 3 different pairs (letter count a, digit count d) meeting all three rules.
y-m-76-10.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a and d, calculate codes, check within both limits (at least 30,000 and at most 600,000).
y-m-76-10.s.s2.hint.1: If outside range, change a or d by one and check again.
y-m-76-10.s.s2.fail.c1: a and d must be integers at least 0.
y-m-76-10.s.s3.prompt: Choose one design and write one advantage and one disadvantage. Use code count number at least once.
y-m-76-10.s.s3.hint.0: Write code count for your chosen design and compare it with needed 30,000.
y-m-76-10.s.s3.hint.1: Compare from another angle with a different design satisfying same rules.
y-m-76-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check chosen code count falls within both rule limits?
y-m-76-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Are advantage and disadvantage from different viewpoints (length, spare capacity, readability)?
y-m-76-10.s.s3.model.0: 2 letters + 2 digits (57,600 codes) length 4, easy to remember. But using 30,000 means nearly half codes used, leaving little spare capacity.
y-m-76-10.s.s3.model.1: 1 letter + 4 digits (240,000 codes) mostly digits, easy to say, but far more than 30,000 needed, so many unused and long digit string to read.
y-m-76-10.s.s3.model.2: With a=2,d=2, there are 57,600 codes, above 30,000; length 4 is short, but many unused, about 27,000.

y-m-76-05.prereq.0: Assumption: introductory task to try after finishing middle-school maths. H1 na only difficulty label for this batch, no be assignment for any class.
y-m-76-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line for the note.
y-m-76-05.title: Water bill for home using 30 m³: where calculation go wrong?
y-m-76-05.goal: When unit price changes by tier, calculate by correctly separating amount each rate applies to, then find several usage amounts meeting condition.
y-m-76-05.material: Imaginary water rate table. Monthly bill = basic fee 2,000원 + usage charge. First 20 m³ cost 600원 per 1 m³; only amount above 20 m³ cost 900원 per m³. Usage counted in whole m³. Below staff calculation for 30 m³ (line numbers start at 1). 2 000 20 600 1 900 30
y-m-76-05.thinking.2: Making several usage amounts meeting condition
y-m-76-05.prereq.1: Calculating bill with multiplication and addition
y-m-76-05.s.s1.hint.0: Which memo line reflected condition 'only for amount above' in rate table?
y-m-76-05.s.s1.hint.1: Split 30 m³ into 20 m³ and excess; multiply each by its rate.
y-m-76-05.s.s1.line.1: 30 m³ is above 20, so multiply all 30 by 900원: 30 × 900 = 27,000원.
y-m-76-05.s.s1.line.3: Therefore bill for 30 m³ usage is 29,000원.
y-m-76-05.s.s1.explain: Line 2 wrong. 900원 applies only to 10 m³ above 20. Correct: 2,000 + 20×600 + 10×900 = 23,000원. Lines 3 and 4 carry forward line 2 value.
y-m-76-05.s.s2.prompt: Without recalculating, what is most reliable reason to suspect 29,000원 is wrong?
y-m-76-05.s.s2.hint.0: Apply memo method separately to 20 m³ and 21 m³.
y-m-76-05.s.s2.hint.1: Find increase for each extra 1 m³ under real rate table and compare.
y-m-76-05.s.s2.o.a: Using memo method, 20 m³ costs 14,000원 and 21 m³ costs 20,900원, sudden jump.
y-m-76-05.s.s2.o.b: Basic fee 2,000원 too small compared with usage charge, so calculation wrong.
y-m-76-05.s.s2.r.b: Comparing basic fee and usage charge sizes has nothing to do with calculation correctness.
y-m-76-05.s.s2.o.c: Rate was stated as 900원, so 30×900 is fine and no reason to suspect it.
y-m-76-05.s.s2.r.c: You multiply at once without reading which part gets that rate.
y-m-76-05.s.s2.explain: Applying same method to 20 m³ and 21 m³, bill jumps 6,900원 when rate changes from 600원 to 900원. This conflicts with rate table where only charge for extra 1 m³ should increase.
y-m-76-05.s.s3.prompt: Give 3 different usage amounts x (m³) where monthly bill at least 25,000원 but below 30,000원.
y-m-76-05.s.s3.hint.0: First find bill for home using 20 m³.
y-m-76-05.s.s3.hint.1: Use added charge per extra m³ to estimate usage amounts for both range ends. 1
y-m-76-05.s.s3.fail.c1: Usage must be integer from 0 to 100.
y-m-76-05.s.s3.explain: Bill through 20 m³ is 14,000원. Above that add 900원 per extra m³: x=33 gives 25,700원 and x=37 gives 29,300원. 32 m³ gives 24,800원 and 38 m³ gives 30,200원, outside range. Any integer 33–37 works. 20 14 000 900 1 33 25 700 37 29 300 32 24 800 38 30 200

y-m-76-04.prereq.0: Assumption: introductory task to try after finishing middle-school maths. H1 na only difficulty label for this batch, no be assignment for any class.
y-m-76-04.title: Screen showed 10.1: pass or fail?
y-m-76-04.topic: Error and tolerance: judging rounded measurement
y-m-76-04.goal: Find range of real values represented by rounded reading; separate cases where pass/fail can be decided from cases where it can't.
y-m-76-04.material: Bolt diameter requirement is '10.00 mm ± 0.08 mm'. Actual x passes if at least 9.92 mm and at most 10.08 mm. Site gauge rounds actual value to nearest 0.1 mm and shows it. Rounding boundaries go up (actual 10.05→screen 10.1; actual 10.04→screen 10.0). So screen 10.0 means actual at least 9.95 and below 10.05.
y-m-76-04.thinking.0: Finding range of actual values represented by screen number
y-m-76-04.prereq.1: Writing absolute value or '± range' as inequality (middle-school level)
y-m-76-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all screen readings where pass or fail can be decided from screen alone.
y-m-76-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each screen value, first write interval where actual value may lie.
y-m-76-04.s.s1.hint.1: Compare interval with passing range 9.92 to 10.08 on number line.
y-m-76-04.s.s1.r.a: You read 9.9 below lower spec limit 9.92, so fail. But actual for screen 9.9 is at least 9.85 and below 9.95, so some values are 9.92 or higher.
y-m-76-04.s.s1.r.b: You didn't check if whole actual interval for screen 10.0 (at least 9.95 and below 10.05) sits inside pass range.
y-m-76-04.s.s1.r.c: You read 10.1 above upper spec 10.08, so fail. But actual for screen 10.1 at least 10.05 and below 10.15, so some values are 10.08 or lower.
y-m-76-04.s.s1.r.d: You didn't check if actual interval for screen 10.2 (at least 10.15 and below 10.25) overlaps passing range.
y-m-76-04.s.s1.explain: Screen 10.0 means actual at least 9.95 and below 10.05, all pass; 10.2 means at least 10.15 and below 10.25, all fail. For 9.9 (9.85–9.95) and 10.1 (10.05–10.15), intervals partly overlap pass range, so can't decide.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.prompt: Suppose tolerance rewritten ±t mm (pass: 10 − t ≤ x ≤ 10 + t). Give 3 different t values where screen 10.0 definitely passes, but screen 10.1 cannot be decided pass/fail. (t to 2 decimals. If it passes only at single boundary point, count as 'definite fail'.)
y-m-76-04.s.s2.hint.0: Compare both ends of actual intervals for screen readings 10.0 and 10.1 with 10+t.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.hint.1: Change t to 0.05, 0.1, 0.15 and see how judgment changes for both screen readings.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.fail.c1: t must be greater than 0 and less than 1, to 2 decimal places.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.ok.c2: Screen 10.0 definitely passes, and at screen 10.1 some actual values can pass.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.fail.c2: If t is 0.05 or less, almost none of actual values for screen 10.1 pass (definite fail).
y-m-76-04.s.s2.ok.c3: At screen 10.1, some actual values still fail.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.fail.c3: If t is 0.15 or more, all actual values for screen 10.1 pass, so it's settled.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.explain: For screen 10.0 to definitely pass, interval end 10.05 must be no more than upper limit 10+t (t≥0.05). For only part of screen 10.1 interval to pass, need 10.05 < 10+t < 10.15. So any 0.05 < t < 0.15 works.
y-m-76-04.s.s3.prompt: How should you handle bolt with screen reading 10.1 (spec 10.00 ± 0.08)? Write action and reason.
y-m-76-04.s.s3.hint.0: First write interval where actual value for screen 10.1 may lie.
y-m-76-04.s.s3.hint.1: Point out parts of interval that pass and parts that fail.
y-m-76-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you mention at least one advantage or disadvantage (time, cost, defect risk) of your choice?
y-m-76-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you directly state actual-value interval represented by screen reading 10.1?
y-m-76-04.s.s3.model.0: Screen 10.1 is rounded, so actual is at least 10.05 and below 10.15. It crosses pass limit 10.08, so measure again with more precise device.
y-m-76-04.s.s3.model.1: Since we can't decide, we can treat it as fail for now and measure to two decimals only pieces that might pass. Choose based on whether scrapping good parts or releasing faulty ones costs more.
y-m-76-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: A variation choosing cautious handling and weighing cost

y-m-76-06.title: Simple interest 5% yearly or compound 4% yearly: which better for long deposit?
y-m-76-06.topic: Simple and compound interest: comparison over time
y-m-76-06.goal: Use period-by-period calculations to check that higher interest rate isn't always better, and make advice for when period unknown.
y-m-76-06.material: At bank counter, explain two choices for depositing principal 1,000,000원. Product P: 5% simple yearly interest (each year add 5% of original amount). Product Q: 4% compound yearly (each year add 4% of previous year's total). Ignore taxes, fees, early withdrawal; interest calculated once yearly and period whole years only. Calculator allowed.
y-m-76-06.prereq.1: Calculating percentages and powers (1.04^n) with calculator
y-m-76-06.prereq.2: Meaning of simple and compound interest: simple adds interest only to original amount; compound adds interest to principal too, so next year interest applies to it.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.prompt: Revise judgment 'which product better' each time another detail arrive.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write difference between amounts for each period and see how it changes.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.hint.1: If difference changes sign, consider what happened in periods between.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.0.info: Only known P rate 5% yearly and Q rate 4%; deposit period unknown.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.0.after: At this stage both choosing higher-rate P and leaving answer open because period unknown have reasons. Choosing Q just because name says compound interest has weak reason.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.1.info: Calculated after 3 years: P 1,150,000원, Q about 1,124,864원.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.1.after: For 3 years, P leads. But that isn't conclusion for every period.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: For 3 years, Q about 25,000원 below P. You read calculation backward.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Amounts differ about 25,000원, so not same.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.info: After 10 years P 1,500,000원; Q about 1,480,244원. Difference about 25,000원 at 3 years, about 20,000원 at 10.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: What judgment from how difference changes?
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.after: P still ahead but gap shrinking. This suggests order may switch over longer time.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.o.a: P stays ahead and difference almost constant.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Gap shrank from 25,000원 to 20,000원; not constant.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.o.b: P leads but gap shrinking, so check longer period.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.o.c: From now on, judge Q better.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: After 10 years P still leads. Too early to change judgment.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.3.after: P leads at 10 years and Q at 20, so order changes between. Higher rate not always better.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.3.o.a: P always better for any period.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.3.r.a: At 20 years Q has about 191,000원 more.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.3.o.b: P better for short time, Q if long enough.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.3.o.c: Two products similar for every period.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.3.r.c: At 20 years gap about 190,000원. Hard to call similar.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.reflect: First both judgments reasonable; as evidence came in (P at 3-year mark, still P but gap shrunk at 10, Q ahead at 20) judgment changed. Say what stage decisive.
y-m-76-06.s.s2.prompt: Give 3 different periods n years when Q maturity (4% compound) exceeds P maturity (5% simple). (n integer up to 30)
y-m-76-06.s.s2.hint.0: Choose period and calculate both amounts with calculator.
y-m-76-06.s.s2.hint.1: Change period gradually to find around when leader changes.
y-m-76-06.s.s2.fail.c2: At this period, Q maturity is no more than P.
y-m-76-06.s.s2.explain: At n=12, Q about 1,601,032원 vs P 1,600,000원, so Q leads first time. At n=11, Q about 1,539,454원 vs P 1,550,000원, so P leads. Any integer 12–30 works.
y-m-76-06.s.s3.prompt: How explain two products to customer who doesn't know period? Include cutoff period and what you would ask.
y-m-76-06.s.s3.hint.0: Find again from above steps when products first switch order.
y-m-76-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write one sentence each for which product better before and after cutoff.
y-m-76-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you ask how long customer plans to deposit?
y-m-76-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say which product leads before and after cutoff?
y-m-76-06.s.s3.model.0: 12 years is turning point. If deposit 12 years or more, compound Q gives more; if shorter, simple P gives more. First ask how many years they plan to keep it.
y-m-76-06.s.s3.model.1: At about 10 years P has about 20,000원 more, but after 12 Q leads. Ask customer 'Can you leave it more than 12 years?' and decide based on answer.

y-m-76-01.title: Finding the original price from "VAT Included" total for receipt
y-m-76-01.topic: Percentages: finding pre-VAT price from amount wey include VAT
y-m-76-01.goal: Understand say the same 10% fit give different amount depending on the base value, then find and correct the wrong line for a calculation note wey find VAT and pre-VAT price from total wey include VAT.
y-m-76-01.material: The price for item wey shop dey sell na "the pre-VAT price (the amount before dem add VAT) plus 10% VAT", and VAT na 10% of pre-VAT price. Receipt show only total of 33,000 won, so one worker write the note below to find VAT and pre-VAT price. No round am, and no consider other tax or cost. (Line numbers start from 1.)
y-m-76-01.thinking.0: Finding the first wrong line for calculation note
y-m-76-01.thinking.1: Checking the base with '10% of wetin'
y-m-76-01.thinking.2: Finding the percentage to subtract from total by yourself
y-m-76-01.prereq.0: Assumption: introductory task to try after finishing middle-school maths. H1 na only difficulty label for this batch, no be assignment for any class.
y-m-76-01.prereq.1: Calculating by changing percentage (%) to decimal and multiplying (first-year junior secondary level)
y-m-76-01.prereq.2: The meaning of cost, list price, and sale price (list price na the selling price wey shop display)
y-m-76-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line for the note.
y-m-76-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, write inside brackets wetin the "10%" na 10% of.
y-m-76-01.s.s1.hint.1: Add VAT again to pre-VAT price for line 3 and check whether e equal the original total.
y-m-76-01.s.s1.line.0: Total of 33,000 won na pre-VAT price plus 10% VAT.
y-m-76-01.s.s1.line.1: VAT na 10% of total, so 33,000 × 0.1 = 3,300 won.
y-m-76-01.s.s1.line.3: Check: add 10% VAT (2,970 won) to 29,700 won = 32,670 won, small difference from total, but we treat am as small matter.
y-m-76-01.s.s1.line.4: On other receipts too, subtract 10% of total to get pre-VAT price, so same method work.
y-m-76-01.s.s1.explain: Line 2 na first mistake. VAT 10% na 10% of pre-VAT price, no be total. Total = pre-VAT price × 1.1, so pre-VAT price = 33,000 ÷ 1.1 = 30,000 won; VAT na 3,000 won. Lines 3 and 4 carry on value from line 2, and line 4 check differ from total (32,670 won). That difference show calculation wrong, but dem ignore am.
y-m-76-01.s.s2.prompt: What is best way to find pre-VAT price from total 33,000 won?
y-m-76-01.s.s2.hint.0: Call pre-VAT price one letter (like x) and write equation showing total in terms of x.
y-m-76-01.s.s2.hint.1: Check if adding 10% VAT again to candidate value give 33,000 won.
y-m-76-01.s.s2.r.a: 10% when increasing is based on pre-VAT price, but 10% when decreasing is based on total, so amounts differ. Add VAT again to value you found and see if you get total.
y-m-76-01.s.s2.r.b: Dis calculation add VAT to total one more time. Pre-VAT price must be lower than total.
y-m-76-01.s.s2.o.c: Total is 1.1 times pre-VAT price, so divide total by 1.1.
y-m-76-01.s.s2.o.d: If you don't know pre-VAT price, you can't find VAT either, so total alone no enough to calculate am.
y-m-76-01.s.s2.r.d: You can find am by treating pre-VAT price as unknown and making equation "total = pre-VAT price × 1.1".
y-m-76-01.s.s2.explain: Total = pre-VAT price + 10% of pre-VAT price = pre-VAT price × 1.1. So pre-VAT price = 33,000 ÷ 1.1 = 30,000 won, VAT 3,000 won. Subtracting 10% of total uses another base and gives wrong answer 29,700 won.
y-m-76-01.s.s3.prompt: What percent of total must you subtract to get pre-VAT price? Find it to 1 decimal place, show calculation and reason.
y-m-76-01.s.s3.hint.0: First find how many won VAT is inside total 33,000 won.
y-m-76-01.s.s3.hint.1: Divide to find what percent of total that amount be.
y-m-76-01.s.s3.placeholder: For example: VAT na ... of total.
y-m-76-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check say applying your rate to total 33,000 won leaves pre-VAT price 30,000 won?
y-m-76-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why it no be 10%, using word 'base'?
y-m-76-01.s.s3.model.0: VAT 3,000 won na 3,000 ÷ 33,000 = about 9.1% of total 33,000 won. Ten percent is based on pre-VAT price; if total is base, rate below 10%. 3 000 33 9.1 10
y-m-76-01.s.s3.model.1: Subtract one-eleventh of total (about 9.1%) to get pre-VAT price. Total is 1.1 times pre-VAT price, so VAT is 1 of 11 parts of total. Take away 10% of total and too much go come out.
y-m-76-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: Variation written with fraction instead of rate

y-m-76-02.prereq.0: Assumption: introductory task to try after finishing middle-school maths. H1 na only difficulty label for this batch, no be assignment for any class.
y-m-76-02.title: Is fixed daily pay or per-delivery pay better?
y-m-76-02.topic: Comparing pay plans with linear expressions
y-m-76-02.goal: Use expressions to check which plan better changes with daily deliveries, then recommend with conditions.
y-m-76-02.material: Delivery worker want choose one of two pay plans. A: 3,500원 per delivery. B: fixed 30,000원 a day plus 2,000원 each delivery. Daily delivery number integer from 0 upward, maximum 60. Ignore tips, fuel and tax.
y-m-76-02.thinking.0: Comparing two plans by delivery count
y-m-76-02.prereq.2: Meaning of inequality and comparing expression sizes
y-m-76-02.s.s1.prompt: Without knowing delivery count per day, what can you say by comparing two plans?
y-m-76-02.s.s1.hint.0: Put 0, 10, 20, 30 deliveries and pay for each plan in table.
y-m-76-02.s.s1.hint.1: Find in table where leading plan changes.
y-m-76-02.s.s1.o.a: A: pay per delivery bigger, so A always earn more no matter delivery count.
y-m-76-02.s.s1.r.a: You look only at per-delivery amount and miss B fixed pay. When delivery count low, fixed part big share.
y-m-76-02.s.s1.o.b: Which plan ahead changes with deliveries, and some delivery count make pay equal.
y-m-76-02.s.s1.o.c: B: fixed amount dey, so B always earn more no matter deliveries.
y-m-76-02.s.s1.r.c: You only look at fixed pay and miss how per-delivery difference adds up as deliveries increase.
y-m-76-02.s.s1.o.d: It can vary with deliveries, but no delivery count make two plans exactly equal.
y-m-76-02.s.s1.r.d: You talk without checking by calculation whether equal point dey. Try few delivery numbers.
y-m-76-02.s.s1.explain: A = 3,500n; B = 30,000 + 2,000n. Difference of 1,500원 each delivery builds up; at n=20 both equal 70,000원. Under 20 deliveries B pays more; above 20 A pays more.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.prompt: Give 3 different daily delivery numbers n where A pays more than B.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.hint.0: Write two expressions using same letter for number of deliveries and compare them.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.hint.1: Find boundary number first, then test some numbers above am.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Number of deliveries must be integer 0 to 60.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.ok.c2: A pay greater than B pay.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.fail.c2: At this delivery count, A pay equal to or below B.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.explain: A leads from 21 deliveries. At 20 both pay 70,000원; below that B higher. Any integer from 21 to 60 works.
y-m-76-02.s.s3.prompt: Which plan recommend to person doing 18 to 24 deliveries daily? Explain with standard delivery count.
y-m-76-02.s.s3.hint.0: First find delivery count where pay equal, then see whether 18 and 24 are above or below.
y-m-76-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check at stated cutoff both plans pay same?
y-m-76-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say which leads at 18 and at 24 deliveries?
y-m-76-02.s.s3.model.0: 20 deliveries is the turning point. Both pay 70,000원 at 20; from 21 A pays more, and at 19 or below B pays more. Average 18 to 24 is about 21, so A slightly better overall, but on an 18-delivery day B safer.
y-m-76-02.s.s3.model.1: If you worry deliveries may drop under 20, B good. Even with many days off, 30,000원 guaranteed. But if you mostly do above 20, A better.
y-m-76-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer splitting recommendation according to conditions

y-m-76-09.prereq.0: Assumption: try after middle-school maths. H2 only difficulty label meaning analysis one step more careful than H1, not grade assignment.
y-m-76-09.title: Is a product with alarm sounding 90% likely to be defective?
y-m-76-09.topic: Conditional probability: connection between alarm and defect
y-m-76-09.goal: Use counts to show 'alarm if defective' differs from 'defective if alarm'; work out how value changes when defect rate changes.
y-m-76-09.material: Factory inspection alarm sounds with 90% probability for defective product, and 5% even for normal product (false alarm). No other way to tell. Defective share among all products can differ by production line.
y-m-76-09.thinking.0: Updating probability judgment with new information
y-m-76-09.thinking.1: Finding several defect rates fitting condition
y-m-76-09.prereq.1: Meaning of probability and expressing as ratio (middle-school level)
y-m-76-09.s.s1.prompt: Revise judgment 'chance product with alarm is actually defective' each time new info arrives.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.hint.0: Split 1,000 items into defective/normal and table how many in each group trigger alarm.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.hint.1: Take only alarmed items and count how many defective.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.info: Only machine performance known (alarm for 90% of defective, 5% of normal). We don't know how common defects are.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is fitting judgment about chance an alarmed product is defective?
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.after: Share defective among alarmed items depends whether defects common or rare, so can't decide from this information alone.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You read 'alarm if defective' probability 90% as 'defective if alarm'.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Can't decide without knowing how common defects are.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.o.c: About 50%, because product either defective or not, one of two.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Two outcomes doesn't mean probabilities are equal.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.1.info: On this line, 20 of 1,000 items (2%) defective. Alarm sounds for 18 of 20 defective (90%) and for 49 of 980 normal (5%).
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: Among alarmed products, what chance is defective?
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.1.after: Among 67 alarmed products, 18 defective, about 26.9%. Where defects rare, false alarms outnumber true alarms.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.1.o.b: About 5%, chance normal product gives false alarm.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.1.r.b: 5% is false-alarm probability among normal products, not defective share among alarmed products.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.2.info: On another line, 100 of 1,000 items (10%) defective. Alarm sounds for 90 of 100 defective and 45 of 900 normal.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.2.ask: How does chance alarmed item is defective here compare with previous line?
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.2.after: Of 135 alarmed items, 90 defective, about 66.7%. Same machine, but more common defects make alarmed item more likely truly defective.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It stays same as previous line, about 27%.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Same machine performance doesn't mean same result. Defect frequency changed.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It gets lower instead, about 10%, the defect rate.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.2.r.c: 10% is only defect rate on this line. Count again among alarmed products only.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.reflect: At first info wasn't enough, so 'can't decide' fit. Once defect rate given, counting gave value; when defect rate changed, value changed greatly. Explain why result changed though machine performance same.
y-m-76-09.s.s2.prompt: Give 3 different defect rates p% where chance alarmed product is defective at least 50%. (p integer 1 to 50; machine performance as above.)
y-m-76-09.s.s2.hint.0: Choose rate and count, out of 100, defective and normal items that trigger alarm.
y-m-76-09.s.s2.hint.1: Find cutoff where alarms among defective exceed alarms among normal.
y-m-76-09.s.s2.fail.c1: Defect rate must be whole-number percent from 1 to 50.
y-m-76-09.s.s2.ok.c2: Chance alarmed product is defective at least 50%.
y-m-76-09.s.s2.fail.c2: Chance alarmed product is defective below 50%.
y-m-76-09.s.s2.explain: If defect rate p%, per 100 items p defective and 0.9p alarm; 100−p normal and 0.05×(100−p) alarm. For defective to be at least half: 0.9p ≥ 0.05×(100−p), so p ≥ about 5.3. As integer, p≥6.
y-m-76-09.s.s3.prompt: Write one-line workplace notice saying what worker should do when alarm sounds, and why alarm doesn't prove defect.
y-m-76-09.s.s3.hint.0: Recall how many alarmed products were normal in earlier steps.
y-m-76-09.s.s3.hint.1: State that fact in one sentence and what to do next.
y-m-76-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Would worker who reads this stop throwing away alarmed products immediately?
y-m-76-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you consider wording may differ for low-defect and high-defect lines?
y-m-76-09.s.s3.model.0: Even if alarm sounds, defect isn't confirmed. It may be false alarm, so set aside and inspect again.
y-m-76-09.s.s3.model.1: On line with low defect rate, many alarmed products may be normal. Don't discard right away; recheck them.

y-m-76-13.prereq.0: Assumption: try after middle-school maths. H2 only difficulty label meaning analysis one step more careful than H1, not grade assignment.
y-m-76-13.title: How many sandwiches prepare: is average demand enough?
y-m-76-13.goal: Compare expected profit for each quantity using demand distribution; add standard like worst case and find amounts meeting conditions.
y-m-76-13.material: Small shop makes and sells sandwiches each morning. Each costs 2,000원 to make and sells for 5,000원. Leftovers thrown away. In last 20 days, demand was 10 on 4 days, 12 on 6 days, 14 on 6 days, 16 on 4 days. Assume same proportions continue. Prepare integer 10 to 16. Daily profit = sold count×5,000 − prepared count×2,000.
y-m-76-13.thinking.0: Considering limit of deciding by mean alone
y-m-76-13.thinking.1: Meeting two standards: expected and worst-case profit
y-m-76-13.prereq.1: Expected value: multiply each value by probability and add (extension of middle-school level)
y-m-76-13.prereq.2: Idea of choosing smaller of two values, like min(prepared amount, demand)
y-m-76-13.s.s1.prompt: Average demand is 13. What is best judgment about choosing preparation amount?
y-m-76-13.s.s1.hint.0: Prepare 13 and 14; write profit for each when demand 10, 12, 14, 16.
y-m-76-13.s.s1.hint.1: Multiply by how often each demand occurs and compare expected profits for both amounts.
y-m-76-13.s.s1.o.a: Preparing 13, equal to average demand, gives highest expected profit.
y-m-76-13.s.s1.r.a: You assumed mean demand equals amount with highest expected profit. If leftover loss and missed-sale profit differ, answer can differ.
y-m-76-13.s.s1.o.b: Because leftover loss and missed profit differ, best preparation amount can differ from mean.
y-m-76-13.s.s1.o.c: Prepare 16, highest demand, so no customers missed.
y-m-76-13.s.s1.r.c: You only consider not missing customers, ignore cost of leftovers.
y-m-76-13.s.s1.explain: When making one more, if sold, profit 3,000원; if unsold, loss 2,000원. These differ, so highest expected-profit amount needn't equal mean 13. Calculation gives 34,500원 for 13 and 35,000원 for 14.
y-m-76-13.s.s2.prompt: Give 2 different quantities q to prepare meeting both: (1) expected profit at least 34,000원; (2) profit at least 22,000원 even when demand is lowest (10). (q integer 10–16)
y-m-76-13.s.s2.hint.0: Choose amount and find profit when demand 10,12,14,16. 10 12 14 16
y-m-76-13.s.s2.hint.1: Multiply each profit by its frequency and add for expected profit, then compare with both conditions.
y-m-76-13.s.s2.fail.c1: Prepared amount must be integer 10 to 16.
y-m-76-13.s.s2.ok.c3: Even when demand 10, profit at least 22,000원.
y-m-76-13.s.s2.explain: Expected profit: q=12 gives 34,000원, 13 gives 34,500원, 14 gives 35,000원. Profit at demand 10: 26,000원, 24,000원, 22,000원. q=11 expected profit 32,000원, fails condition 1; q=15 and 16 worst-day profits 20,000원 and 18,000원, fail condition 2.
y-m-76-13.s.s3.prompt: Recommend a preparation amount to shop. Choose a number and cite expected profit or worst-day profit; say whether recommendation can change with risk attitude.
y-m-76-13.s.s3.hint.0: Put expected profit and lowest-demand-day profit side by side for two candidate quantities.
y-m-76-13.s.s3.hint.1: Find point where choice splits by how much you want to avoid risk.
y-m-76-13.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you match chosen amount's expected profit to values above?
y-m-76-13.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say recommendation may differ for people more or less risk-averse?
y-m-76-13.s.s3.model.0: I recommend 14. Highest expected profit is 35,000원. But on low-demand day (10) profit falls to 22,000원; if that risk bothers you, reduce to 12.
y-m-76-13.s.s3.model.1: I recommend 12. Expected profit 34,000원, only 1,000원 below 14; even with demand 10, 26,000원 remains, so safer.
y-m-76-13.s.s3.modelNote.1: Variation choosing the less risky option
